title: BallisticMissileClear
question: What is a ballistic missile?
hook: A ballistic missile is a rocket that pushes for a few minutes and then simply falls, along the same kind of arc as a thrown ball. Fire Newton's cannon on a curved Earth and watch an arc close into an orbit.

explainer.title: One push, then free fall
explainer.text: Ballistic means moving under gravity alone after a single push, like a thrown ball. A ballistic missile is a rocket whose engine burns only for the first few minutes; then it coasts on a free-fall arc and falls back into the air.

explainer.title: Newton's cannon
explainer.text: Newton imagined a cannon on a mountain above the air. Faster shots land further round the curve of the Earth. At about 7.9 km/s the ground curves away as fast as the ball falls, and it orbits. At about 11.2 km/s it escapes.

explainer.title: Every arc is part of an ellipse
explainer.text: A free-fall path around the Earth is a piece of an ellipse with the Earth's centre at one focus, the same shape Kepler found for planets. A short arc is the top of a long, thin ellipse that runs into the ground.

explainer.title: Powered by rockets
explainer.text: The push comes from a rocket built in stages that drop away when empty. Sounding rockets, satellite launchers and ballistic missiles all share this rocket physics; only the path differs.

explainer.title: Names and ranges
explainer.text: The Arms Control Association sorts ballistic missiles into short-range (under 1,000 km), medium-range (1,000 to 3,000 km), intermediate-range (3,000 to 5,500 km) and intercontinental (over 5,500 km). Cruise missiles are different: they fly like aircraft.

explainer.title: The human cost and the treaties
explainer.text: By the end of 1945 the atomic bombings had killed about 140,000 people in Hiroshima and 70,000 in Nagasaki. Since then the NPT, the INF Treaty, the MTCR, the CTBT and New START have tried to limit these weapons, with mixed success.

concepts.def: Moving under gravity alone after the push has ended, like a thrown ball or a cannon shell.
Motion with only gravity acting. A thrown ball, a coasting rocket and an orbiting satellite are all in free fall.
The three phases of a ballistic flight: the engine burns, the rocket coasts on its arc, then it falls back into the air.
About 7.9 km/s at the Earth's surface: fast enough sideways that the ground curves away as fast as you fall.
About 11.2 km/s from the Earth's surface: fast enough to leave the Earth for good.
A stretched circle. Every free-fall path round the Earth is part of one, with the Earth's centre at a focus.
The glow of air squeezed and heated in front of anything that falls back into the air very fast.
A missile that flies like a small aircraft, held up by wings with its engine running all the way.
Agreements between countries to limit, check or reduce weapons, such as the NPT and New START.
